title_ar: ماذاعن قول الصاوي بأن الأخذ بظاهر الكتاب و السنة أصل من أصول الكفر؟
title_en: What of al-Sawi's Statement That Taking the Apparent Meaning of the Book and the Sunnah Is One of the Roots of Unbelief?
body_ar:
عن قول الصاوي بأن الأخذ بظاهر الكتاب و السنة أصل من أصول الكفر؟

هذا كلام غير صحيح أصلا و أنه أيضا مع ذلك غير أديب لأن الله سبحانه و تعالى لم يرسل إلينا الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم بالألغاز و إنما أرسله إلينا بالوحي المبين الواضح الميسر للذكر الذي قال فيه: ﴿و لقد يسرنا القرآن للذكر فهل من مدكر﴾ و لم يكن ليرسل إلينا بأمور لا نفهمها و لا تصل إليها عقولنا و لكن الكلام إنما هو فيما يتخيل الإنسان أنه ظاهر النص و ليس كذلك فمثلا كثير من الناس إذا سمع إثبات صفة من صفات الله تعالى انطبع في ذهنه اتصاف المخلوق بذلك فدعاه هذا إلى التشبيه و التجسيم و هذا ليس هو ظاهر الآية و إنما هو التصور الذي في ذهنه هو فقط فلذلك الغلط من فهمه هو لا من النص و من أجل هذا يجب عليه أن يعلم أن الذي فهمه غير معنى الآية و غير ظاهرها بل هو فهم اتصاف الخالق بصفة المخلوق على هيئة اتصاف المخلوق بذلك و هذا مخالف لمعنى النص و مخالف لظاهره.
body_en:
On al-Sawi's statement that taking the apparent meaning (ẓāhir) of the Book and the Sunnah is one of the roots of unbelief?

This is speech that is not correct at all, and along with that it is also discourteous — because God, glorified and exalted, did not send the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to us with riddles. He sent him to us rather with the clear and plain revelation, made easy for remembrance, of which He said: {And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance; so is there any who will remember?} (Sūrat al-Qamar 54:17). He would not send to us matters that we do not understand and that our intellects cannot reach.

But what is at issue is only in what a person imagines to be the apparent sense of the text when it is not so. For example: many people, when they hear the affirmation of one of the attributes of God, exalted, have impressed upon their minds the creature's having that same attribute, and this leads them to likening God to creation (tashbīh) and to ascribing a body to Him (tajsīm). But this is not the apparent sense of the verse; it is only the conception that is in his own mind. The error is therefore from his own understanding, not from the text. For this reason he is obliged to know that what he understood is other than the meaning of the verse and other than its apparent sense; rather what he understood is that the Creator has an attribute of the creature in the very manner in which the creature has it — and this is contrary to the meaning of the text and contrary to its apparent sense.

flags.arabic: هذا كلام غير صحيح أصلا و أنه أيضا مع ذلك غير أديب
flags.context: the Sheikh's verdict on the statement attributed to al-Sawi
options: not correct at all, and along with that also discourteous
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW. Ahmad al-Sawi is a Maliki commentator of great standing, and this is the Sheikh — himself a Maliki — rejecting a much-quoted sentence of his in blunt terms, including a judgement on its manners and not only its content. The sentence at issue is itself among the most polemicised lines in modern Islamic controversy, quoted constantly in disputes between Sufi-Ash'ari and Salafi currents. Translated faithfully, neither softened nor sharpened. Note carefully what the Sheikh does NOT do: he does not accuse al-Sawi of anything, he does not enter the wider controversy, and he immediately turns to explaining what he thinks the underlying concern really is. The English must not let the opening sentence stand as the whole of his answer, and the publication decision belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.context: the term the whole answer turns on, used five times
options: apparent meaning / apparent sense (ẓāhir), kept uniform throughout
flags.note: ẓāhir is fixed in the glossary as 'apparent meaning' and has been kept uniform across all five occurrences, because the Sheikh's entire argument is a distinction between the genuine ẓāhir of a text and what a reader imagines its ẓāhir to be. Rendering it as 'literal meaning' would collapse that distinction and hand the argument to the position he is rejecting.

flags.arabic: إثبات صفة من صفات الله تعالى … التشبيه و التجسيم
flags.context: the example the Sheikh gives of a misread apparent sense
options: the affirmation of one of the attributes of God; likening God to creation (tashbīh) and ascribing a body to Him (tajsīm)
establishing a divine attribute; anthropomorphism and corporealism
proving an attribute of God; comparison and embodiment
flags.note: STYLE GUIDE §8 APPLIES. This is a creedal passage about the divine attributes, not a passage of legal rulings, and none of the five-rulings vocabulary may be read into it. tashbīh and tajsīm are technical terms of kalām; the single-word English equivalents in option 2 are usable but carry European philosophical freight, so the Arabic has been kept alongside a plain rendering.

flags.context: the title as against the first line of the body
options: preserve both source forms and flag
normalise the title's ماذاعن to ماذا عن
supply ماذا at the head of the body
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT. The title runs two words together as ماذاعن, and the body's opening line drops the interrogative ماذا altogether, so that the body's question begins 'On al-Sawi's statement …' with no question word. Both are preserved as the source has them; nothing has been supplied. The English opening line reads as the fragment it is.

The Qur'anic quotation is given in the source without a reference; the reference has been supplied per house style. The wording matches Sūrat al-Qamar 54:17.

al-Sawi is named in the source by surname alone and is romanised without diacritics in body text per house style. The work in which the disputed sentence appears is not named by the Sheikh and has not been supplied.
The Sheikh does not say in this record what the correct handling of the attribute verses is; he says only what the error is not. That limit has been kept.
